items.prompt: Dev (in informal-authority) needed to win one steering-committee meeting within twelve days. Yuki needs 14 teams to adopt her service-boundary approach over the next year, with no meeting where it gets decided. What's the key difference in what 'winning' means for each of them?
choices: Nothing — both are solved by winning one well-timed meeting
Dev needed to win a single room on a single day; Yuki needs her position to become the default across many decisions she won't be present for
Yuki's problem is easier because she has more time
Dev's problem doesn't require any influence at all, just a good argument
items.explanation: Dev's problem had a single decisive moment: one meeting, one sign-off, a small group of named people. Yuki's doesn't — the actual decisions happen fourteen separate times, on fourteen different schedules, mostly without her present. 'Winning' for her means becoming the default reached for by people making decisions on their own, not agreement in a shared room.
items.reference:
Single-decision influence

One room, one moment, a small named group

Org-level influence

Many decisions, over months, mostly without you present

Why: 'winning' means something different at each scale — a room agreeing on a day vs. becoming the default other people reach for.
items.learnMore:
Single-decision vs. org-level influence

The same underlying skill — getting a decision you don't own to go a certain way — plays out very differently depending on the shape of the decision.

Single-decisionOrg-level
ShapeOne moment, one roomMany decisions over months
Main toolA coalition built before the meetingDurable artifacts and reputation
Time horizonDays to weeksMonths to years

Org-level influence means becoming the default people reach for when you aren't in the room to argue for it.

Common mistake

Treating a strong all-hands presentation as equivalent to winning a coalition vote. It raises awareness, but most of the real decisions still happen later, without you present.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest sign an influence problem is org-level rather than single-decision?

The person trying to influence has a senior title
The topic is technical rather than a business one
items.explanation: A single-decision problem has a clear moment — a date, a room, a small named group. An org-level problem has no such moment; it's many separate decisions spread across people and time, most of which the influencer will never be in the room for. That's what makes durable artifacts and reputation the load-bearing tools, instead of a coalition built for one meeting.

items.prompt: Yuki could just tell each tech lead her opinion in a Slack message instead of writing an RFC. What's the main thing a written RFC does that the message doesn't?
choices: Nothing meaningful — both communicate the same idea
It can be found and cited later by someone who was never part of the original conversation
It's required by company policy
It takes less time to write
items.explanation: A Slack message lives in one thread, seen once. A durable artifact like an RFC is built to be found later, by someone who wasn't part of the original conversation, at the exact moment they need it — that's what makes it durable rather than just written down.
items.reference:
💬 A conversation ends when the conversation ends
📄 A durable artifact keeps being found and cited long after

Why: the artifact's job is carrying the reasoning far enough that a stranger can apply it correctly, not just announcing a verdict.
items.learnMore:
Durable artifacts

An RFC, design doc, or ADR keeps making the case long after the conversation that produced it has been forgotten.

ConversationDurable artifact
Findable later?NoYes — searchable, linked
Citable by a stranger?NoYes — 'see RFC-014'

The artifact's real job is carrying the reasoning, including rejected alternatives, far enough that someone who never met the author can extend it correctly to a case it doesn't literally cover.

Common mistake

Writing a verdict with no reasoning. It only works for cases that look exactly like the example — anything else gets treated as outside its scope.

Trust compounds from being visibly right over time, which a single event can't substitute for
Presentations are against company policy

📉 Being wrong, or opining outside your expertise, spends it back down

items.learnMore:
Reputation as a compounding, spendable account

Trust isn't earned by being right once — it builds from a track record visible over time, and it can be spent down, not just accumulated.

ActionEffect on the account

Common mistake

Assuming a strong track record on one topic licenses full confidence on any topic. It doesn't — it can still be spent down by being wrong somewhere unrelated.

items.prompt: What does 'seeding' an idea mean, in the context of org-level influence?
choices: Announcing the idea for the first time at the exact moment a decision is being made
Introducing the idea in low-stakes ways well before it's needed, so it's already familiar when a real decision arrives
Requiring every team to attend a briefing before making any decision
Keeping the idea private until you have formal authority to enforce it
items.explanation: Seeding means introducing an idea before it's needed — a comment, an aside, a mention in an unrelated context — so that by the time a real decision comes up, the idea is already familiar rather than brand new.
items.reference:
⏰ Introduced cold, mid-decision → reads as a costly detour
🌱 Introduced months earlier, low-stakes → already familiar when it matters

Why: a familiar idea feels like confirming something half-remembered, not adopting a stranger's agenda under time pressure.
items.learnMore:
Seeding ideas before they're needed

By the time someone is actively deciding, under time pressure, with a design half-formed, a brand-new idea is a hard sell — no matter how good it is.

TimingWhat happens
The moment a design is being decidedReads as a costly, unplanned detour
Months earlier, low-stakesFamiliar by the time it matters — feels like confirming, not adopting

Seeding doesn't ask for a decision — a review comment, a five-minute aside, a line in an unrelated doc — it just makes the idea recognizable ahead of time.

Common mistake

Saving a good idea for the moment it's needed, assuming the strength of the idea will carry a cold pitch. Timing determines whether it even gets a fair hearing.

The idea needs to be approved by a VP first

items.prompt: Why is 'weighing in on every architecture question' a losing strategy for someone trying to build company-wide influence, even if every individual opinion is correct?
choices: Being correct too often makes people resentful
Time, attention, and credibility are all finite — spreading them across everything leaves too little concentrated anywhere to actually become a default
Company policy limits how many opinions one person can share
It isn't a losing strategy — more opinions shared always means more influence
items.explanation: Correctness alone doesn't make an opinion stick as a company-wide default — that takes sustained attention and credibility, both of which are finite. Spreading them across every disagreement means no single idea gets enough backing to actually become the default other people reach for.
items.reference:
⏳ Time, attention, and reputation are all finite, spendable resources
🎯 Spending them everywhere leaves too little anywhere to actually stick

Why: a few well-backed bets can reach real adoption; many thinly-backed ones usually can't.
items.learnMore:
A finite influence budget

Time, attention, and credibility are all limited — spending them on every disagreement leaves nothing concentrated enough to move a company-wide default.

ApproachResult
Weigh in on everythingEach opinion gets too thin a slice of time and credibility to stick
Choose a few company-wide betsEnough sustained attention per bet to actually cross the adoption threshold

Picking a few bets isn't caution — it's the only way any of them get enough sustained attention to survive without the person actively pushing them.

Common mistake

Assuming more influence attempts always produce more wins. Past a real limit, backing more bets at once produces fewer durable wins, not more.

items.prompt: Yuki has 120 hours a year of realistic influence budget, and a bet needs roughly 30 hours to reach durable adoption. If she splits her time evenly across 6 bets at once, roughly how many hours does each one get, and what does that suggest about the outcome?

Assuming reputation is unrelated across bets, so a miss on one costs nothing toward the others. It's topic-adjacent, not fully separable.

items.prompt: Suppose Yuki, instead of writing a reasoned RFC, had gotten a VP to simply announce 'all new services must follow domain boundaries' at an all-hands. Why would this likely fail to hold up over the eighteen months, even though it sounds more forceful?
choices: It wouldn't fail — a VP mandate is always stronger than a written RFC

A mandate only binds the room and moment it was announced in; it doesn't carry the reasoning needed for a team to correctly apply it to a case not explicitly covered, and it doesn't survive the VP moving on or people forgetting
VPs aren't allowed to make announcements like this
The mandate would work exactly as well as the RFC, just faster
items.explanation: A verbal mandate is powerful in the room where it's announced, but it doesn't travel — it carries no reasoning for someone to apply to an unanticipated case, and it doesn't survive past the moment unless it's backed by something durable and discoverable, which is exactly what the RFC provides and a one-time announcement doesn't.

Treating a mandate as a substitute for a durable artifactOnly binds the room it was announced in
Backing every opinion instead of a few betsSpreads a finite budget too thin to cross the adoption threshold

Why: both failure modes trade a durable, scalable win for one that doesn't survive past a single moment or a single person's attention.
items.learnMore:
Failure modes at org scale

The failure modes at this scale share a pattern: each one trades a durable, scalable win for something that only works while the person is actively present or actively spending attention.

Failure modeWhy it doesn't scale
A mandate instead of a reasoned artifactDoesn't survive the person leaving or the room forgetting
Backing every opinion at onceNo single bet gets enough sustained attention to cross the adoption threshold
Ignoring public disagreementUnresolved visible disagreement about a durable artifact stays visible

Each failure mode looks like a shortcut in the moment but removes exactly the property — durability, or concentrated attention — that org-level influence depends on.

Common mistake

Assuming a title or a mandate is a faster substitute for a reasoned, durable artifact. It's faster in the moment and weaker over any real time horizon.

items.prompt: Which of these outcomes would most clearly indicate Yuki has fallen into the 'backing every opinion instead of a few bets' failure mode?
choices: Nine of fourteen teams adopting domain boundaries by month 18, with the other five simply not having touched relevant code yet
Yuki actively writing RFCs, seeding conversations, and following up on eleven different architecture opinions simultaneously, with none reaching real adoption after a year
Yuki declining to weigh in on the team's test-framework choice when asked
A recognized specialist publicly disagreeing with one of Yuki's three chosen bets
items.explanation: Spreading real effort across eleven simultaneous opinions with none crossing into real, durable adoption is exactly the failure mode of a budget spread too thin — the other three options either describe a normal, expected outcome or a single manageable event, not the pattern of the failure mode itself.
